soilRecords.name: Alluvial Soil
soilRecords.description: Nutrient-rich river deposits with a balanced texture. A versatile foundation for many food crops.
soilRecords.alt: Freshly cultivated brown earth in a plowed field

soilRecords.name: Black Soil
soilRecords.description: Rich, clayey soil that holds moisture well. A natural choice for cotton and oilseeds.
soilRecords.alt: A close-up of rich, dark brown soil

soilRecords.name: Red Soil
soilRecords.description: Earth with an iron-rich red tone. Organic matter helps this porous soil support healthy growth.
soilRecords.alt: Reddish, rocky soil with a coarse natural texture

soilRecords.name: Sandy Soil
soilRecords.description: Loose, light-textured soil that warms quickly. Suits crops adapted to good drainage.
soilRecords.alt: Fine, light-colored sand with a rippled texture

soilRecords.name: Laterite Soil
soilRecords.description: Weathered tropical soil, often acidic. Selected crops thrive with the right soil amendments.
soilRecords.alt: Rough, coarse earth illustrating a weathered soil texture

soilRecords.name: Loamy Soil
soilRecords.description: A helpful blend of sand, silt, and clay. Holds nutrients while allowing excess water to drain.
soilRecords.alt: Young green seedlings emerging from cultivated brown soil

soilRecords.name: Clay Soil
soilRecords.description: Fine particles hold water and nutrients. Drainage management helps suitable crops flourish.
soilRecords.alt: Dry earth showing the cracks typical of a clay-rich surface

rice.name: Rice
rice.description: A staple grain for warm climates with reliable water and moisture-retentive soil.
rice.alt: A farmer harvesting rice in a green paddy field

blast.name: Blast
blast.description: A disease of leaves and panicle necks that can interrupt grain filling.
symptoms: Spindle-shaped leaf lesions with gray centers and brown borders.
Darkened panicle necks, broken necks, or poorly filled grains.
blast.cause: The fungus Pyricularia oryzae, also known as Magnaporthe oryzae.
blast.conditions: Long periods of leaf wetness, humid weather, dense growth, and excessive nitrogen favor infection.
prevention: Use locally recommended resistant varieties and healthy seed.
Apply balanced nutrition and avoid excessive nitrogen; manage volunteer rice and infected residues.
management: Scout leaves and panicle necks during humid spells.
Seek a local diagnosis promptly if neck infection appears; review irrigation and nutrition with an agricultural adviser.

sheath-blight.name: Sheath Blight
sheath-blight.description: Oval lesions develop on leaf sheaths and can spread upward through the canopy.
symptoms: Gray-green or brown oval lesions near the water line.
Joined lesions, premature leaf drying, and lodging in severe cases.
sheath-blight.cause: Rhizoctonia solani, a fungus that survives in soil and infected plant material.
sheath-blight.conditions: Warm, humid weather, high plant density, and heavy nitrogen use encourage spread.
prevention: Use suitable spacing and balanced fertilizer.
Manage infected residues and avoid moving contaminated plant material between fields.
management: Check lower sheaths and monitor how far lesions spread upward.
Discuss canopy and water management with a local adviser before choosing any crop-protection product.

bacterial-leaf-blight.name: Bacterial Leaf Blight
bacterial-leaf-blight.description: Leaf-edge blight that can reduce the plant area available for grain production.
symptoms: Water-soaked streaks from leaf tips or edges that become yellow-white.
Wavy lesion edges; seedlings may wilt severely in early infections.
bacterial-leaf-blight.cause: Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae, a bacterial pathogen of rice.
bacterial-leaf-blight.conditions: Stormy, wet weather, damaged leaves, and excess nitrogen are associated with outbreaks.
prevention: Choose locally resistant varieties and healthy nursery plants.
Avoid unnecessary seedling clipping and keep nursery tools clean.
management: Have leaf symptoms distinguished from nutrient stress and other blights.
Do not carry water or affected nursery plants into clean fields; follow local extension advice.

brown-spot.name: Brown Spot
brown-spot.description: Small brown spots may become numerous on stressed rice plants.
symptoms: Round to oval brown spots, often with grayish centers.
Spotting on grain coverings and premature leaf drying.
brown-spot.cause: Bipolaris oryzae, a seed- and residue-associated fungus.
brown-spot.conditions: High humidity combined with poor nutrition or moisture stress can increase disease.
prevention: Use healthy seed and improve balanced crop nutrition based on soil tests.
Maintain appropriate irrigation and manage infected residues.
management: Assess nutrition and moisture stress as well as the disease.
Seek advice on seed health and future variety choice rather than relying on visual symptoms alone.

wheat.name: Wheat
wheat.description: A cool-season grain that grows well in fertile, well-drained soils.
wheat.alt: Ripe golden wheat heads in a sunlit field

stem-rust.name: Stem Rust
stem-rust.description: Rust-colored pustules can weaken stems and reduce grain quality.
symptoms: Elongated reddish-brown pustules on stems and leaf sheaths.
Torn plant surfaces around pustules; later pustules can turn black.
stem-rust.cause: Puccinia graminis f. sp. tritici, the wheat stem-rust fungus.
stem-rust.conditions: Warm temperatures with dew or leaf wetness favor infection and windborne spread.
prevention: Grow locally recommended rust-resistant varieties.
Sow within the recommended window and manage volunteer cereal plants.
management: Report early pustules to local extension staff, especially during regional alerts.
Confirm the rust type before acting; stem, leaf, and stripe rust are different diseases.

loose-smut.name: Loose Smut
loose-smut.description: Infected ears are replaced by powdery black spores instead of grain.
symptoms: Most grain-bearing parts of an ear are replaced by a black spore mass.
After spores blow away, a bare central stalk remains.
loose-smut.cause: Ustilago tritici; infection can remain inside apparently healthy seed.
loose-smut.conditions: Moist, mild weather at flowering favors infection of developing seed.
prevention: Use certified healthy seed and locally recommended resistant varieties.
Do not save seed from a field with loose-smut infection.
management: There is no way to restore an already smutted ear.
Ask an adviser about approved seed-health measures for the next sowing.

powdery-mildew.name: Powdery Mildew
powdery-mildew.description: Powdery fungal colonies on leaves reduce healthy green leaf area.
symptoms: White powdery patches on leaves and sheaths.
Older patches turn gray and may contain tiny black structures.
powdery-mildew.cause: Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici, a wheat-specific powdery-mildew fungus.
powdery-mildew.conditions: Cool to mild weather, humidity, dense stands, and excessive nitrogen favor mildew.
prevention: Select resistant varieties where available.
Use recommended seed rates and balanced nitrogen.
management: Monitor upper leaves as grain formation approaches.
Improve crop stress management and ask about local thresholds before considering protection products.

sugarcane.name: Sugarcane
sugarcane.description: A long-duration tropical crop that benefits from deep soil and consistent moisture.
sugarcane.alt: Green sugarcane growing beneath a blue sky

red-rot.name: Red Rot
red-rot.description: An internal stalk infection that affects cane quality and stand survival.
symptoms: Red internal stalk tissue with characteristic white cross-bands.
Drying of the top leaves; split stalks may have a sour smell.
red-rot.cause: Colletotrichum falcatum, a fungus carried in infected planting setts and crop residues.
red-rot.conditions: Susceptible varieties, infected seed cane, wet conditions, and stalk injury increase risk.
prevention: Use certified disease-free planting material and recommended varieties.
Avoid ratooning heavily infected crops and keep planting tools clean.
management: Have suspect stalks examined; similar red discoloration has other causes.
Remove affected clumps according to local recommendations and avoid distributing their setts.

smut.name: Smut
smut.description: A distinctive black whip emerges from infected growing points.
symptoms: A long black whip-like growth at the shoot tip.
Thin stalks and excessive grassy tillering.
smut.cause: Sporisorium scitamineum, a fungus spread through spores and infected setts.
smut.conditions: Susceptible varieties and infected seed cane support repeated outbreaks.
prevention: Plant healthy setts from a reliable source.
Use resistant varieties and inspect seed-cane nurseries.
management: Avoid disturbing mature spore whips in clean planting areas.
Follow local instructions for roguing infected clumps and replacing affected ratoons.

mosaic.name: Mosaic
mosaic.description: A mottled leaf pattern can indicate infection that reduces cane vigor.
symptoms: Alternating light and dark green areas along leaves.
Stunting or reduced growth in susceptible varieties.
mosaic.cause: Sugarcane mosaic virus and related viruses; some are spread by aphids and infected setts.
mosaic.conditions: Infected planting material and nearby virus hosts contribute to spread.
prevention: Use virus-tested planting material where available.
Manage volunteer and weed hosts and inspect nursery plants.
management: There is no treatment that clears a virus from an infected cane.
Prioritize clean planting material, confirmed diagnosis, and local vector-management advice.

maize.name: Maize
maize.description: A versatile grain for food and feed, suited to fertile soils with good drainage.
maize.alt: Green maize plants growing in an agricultural field

northern-leaf-blight.name: Northern Leaf Blight
northern-leaf-blight.description: Long leaf lesions can reduce the green canopy during grain formation.
symptoms: Long, cigar-shaped gray-green to tan lesions.
Lesions may merge and dry large portions of leaves.
northern-leaf-blight.cause: Exserohilum turcicum, a fungus surviving on infected maize residues.
northern-leaf-blight.conditions: Mild temperatures, prolonged dew, and frequent rain favor infection.
prevention: Use resistant hybrids and rotate with non-host crops.
Manage infected crop residues and maintain balanced nutrition.
management: Scout before and around tasseling, including lower leaves.
Ask an adviser to assess severity and variety susceptibility before intervention.

downy-mildew.name: Downy Mildew
downy-mildew.description: Systemic infection can produce striped leaves and abnormal growth.
symptoms: Yellow or pale stripes and stunted plants.
Downy growth beneath leaves during humid mornings; malformed tassels may develop.
downy-mildew.cause: A complex of Peronosclerospora and related oomycete pathogens, depending on region.
downy-mildew.conditions: Humid nights, moisture on foliage, susceptible hybrids, and infected nearby hosts.
prevention: Choose locally resistant hybrids and healthy seed.
Manage volunteer maize and recommended alternate hosts.
management: Confirm the local downy-mildew type with an expert.
Remove severely affected plants following extension guidance and review the next planting plan.

common-rust.name: Common Rust
common-rust.description: Small rusty pustules appear on both sides of maize leaves.
symptoms: Scattered cinnamon-brown pustules on upper and lower leaf surfaces.
Yellowing and drying when leaves become heavily affected.
common-rust.cause: Puccinia sorghi, the common-rust fungus of maize.
common-rust.conditions: Mild weather, humidity, and dew favor infection.
prevention: Grow resistant hybrids and avoid excessive crop stress.
Monitor young plants when rust is reported locally.
management: Distinguish common rust from southern rust and other leaf spots.
Use local risk advice to decide whether additional management is justified.

pulses.name: Pulses
pulses.description: A short-duration, protein-rich legume. This guide focuses on green gram.
pulses.alt: A close view of harvested green mung beans

yellow-mosaic.name: Yellow Mosaic
yellow-mosaic.description: Yellow mottling can sharply reduce growth and pod production.
symptoms: Irregular bright yellow patches mixed with green leaf tissue.
Stunting and fewer, poorly filled pods in early infections.
yellow-mosaic.cause: Mungbean yellow mosaic viruses, transmitted by whiteflies.
yellow-mosaic.conditions: High whitefly pressure and nearby infected legume or weed hosts.
prevention: Use locally resistant varieties and healthy seed.
Protect young plants and manage weed hosts and whiteflies using local integrated practices.
management: There is no curative treatment for infected plants.
Seek confirmation early and manage sources of infection and vectors rather than spraying for a viral cure.

powdery-mildew.name: Powdery Mildew
powdery-mildew.description: White powdery colonies may spread across leaves and pods.
symptoms: White powder on leaves, stems, and sometimes pods.
Premature leaf yellowing and drying during heavy infection.
powdery-mildew.cause: Powdery-mildew fungi, commonly Erysiphe species on green gram.
powdery-mildew.conditions: Mild temperatures, humid nights, and dense foliage favor disease.
prevention: Choose suitable sowing dates and resistant varieties where recommended.
Maintain spacing and avoid excessive vegetative growth.
management: Scout regularly during flowering and pod formation.
Maintain balanced crop nutrition and obtain locally appropriate management advice.

cercospora-leaf-spot.name: Cercospora Leaf Spot
cercospora-leaf-spot.description: Brown leaf spots can join together and lead to premature defoliation.
symptoms: Brown to gray leaf spots with darker borders.
Yellowing and shedding of heavily affected leaves.
cercospora-leaf-spot.cause: Cercospora and related leaf-spot fungi affecting green gram.
cercospora-leaf-spot.conditions: Warm, wet conditions and repeated legume cropping increase risk.
prevention: Use clean seed and rotate with suitable non-host crops.
Reduce leaf wetness and manage infected residues.
management: Track whether spotting is increasing on newly formed leaves.
Have the cause confirmed before choosing a treatment, as bacterial and fungal spots can resemble one another.

cotton.name: Cotton
cotton.description: A warm-season fibre crop that thrives in deep, moisture-retentive black soils.
cotton.alt: Cotton being harvested from a field with open white bolls

fusarium-wilt.name: Fusarium Wilt
fusarium-wilt.description: A soil-borne infection that disrupts water movement inside the plant.
symptoms: Yellowing and wilting, often beginning with lower leaves.
Brown discoloration inside the stem and plant death in patches.
fusarium-wilt.cause: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. vasinfectum; root injury and nematodes may increase damage.
fusarium-wilt.conditions: Warm soil, susceptible varieties, repeated cotton cropping, and root stress.
prevention: Choose resistant varieties and healthy seed.
Avoid carrying soil from affected fields and use locally suitable crop rotations.
management: Distinguish infectious wilt from waterlogging and sudden physiological wilt.
Improve drainage and seek advice on root health; severely affected plants may not recover.

bacterial-blight.name: Bacterial Blight
bacterial-blight.description: Angular leaf spots and dark stem lesions can affect plant health and bolls.
symptoms: Water-soaked angular spots bounded by leaf veins.
Dark stem lesions and lesions on bolls in severe infections.
bacterial-blight.cause: Xanthomonas citri pv. malvacearum, a seed- and residue-associated bacterium.
bacterial-blight.conditions: Warm, wet weather, wind-driven rain, and infected seed.
prevention: Use certified healthy seed and resistant varieties.
Keep field tools clean and manage infected crop residues.
management: Avoid handling wet affected plants when possible.
Have symptoms confirmed and use local recommendations rather than treating it as a fungal disease.

boll-rot.name: Boll Rot
boll-rot.description: Wet conditions and injuries can allow developing cotton bolls to decay.
symptoms: Soft or discolored bolls, sometimes with visible fungal growth.
Stained lint and bolls that fail to open normally.
boll-rot.cause: Several fungi and bacteria can cause boll rot, often following insect injury.
boll-rot.conditions: Rain during boll development, dense growth, and poor air movement.
prevention: Avoid excessive nitrogen and maintain a manageable canopy.
Manage boll-feeding pests using local integrated pest-management guidance.
management: Inspect damaged bolls to identify the underlying cause.
Harvest mature open bolls promptly when conditions permit and separate damaged material.

leaf-curl.name: Leaf Curl
leaf-curl.description: A whitefly-associated viral disease that distorts growth and reduces yield.
symptoms: Upward or downward leaf curling with thickened veins.
Leaf-like growths beneath leaves, stunting, and poor boll development.
leaf-curl.cause: Cotton leaf curl begomoviruses and associated satellite molecules, spread by whiteflies.
leaf-curl.conditions: High whitefly populations, infected surrounding hosts, and susceptible varieties.
prevention: Use recommended tolerant varieties and manage alternate hosts.
Monitor and manage whiteflies with locally advised integrated methods.
management: A virus-infected plant cannot be made virus-free by a spray.
Focus on preventing spread and get local advice before removing plants or treating vectors.

soybean.name: Soybean
soybean.description: A useful oilseed and protein crop for well-drained, moisture-retentive fields.
soybean.alt: Lush soybean plants in a green agricultural field

rust.name: Rust
rust.description: Leaf rust can cause rapid defoliation during humid weather.
symptoms: Small tan or reddish-brown lesions, especially on lower leaves.
Tiny pustules beneath leaves and premature leaf drop.
rust.cause: Phakopsora pachyrhizi and, in some regions, related soybean rust fungi.
rust.conditions: Extended leaf wetness, moderate temperatures, and nearby infected hosts.
prevention: Choose locally recommended varieties and sowing dates.
Monitor regional rust reports and avoid dense, poorly ventilated stands.
management: Examine leaf undersides and request confirmation of suspect rust.
Follow local scouting thresholds and integrated disease advice.

charcoal-rot.name: Charcoal Rot
charcoal-rot.description: Root and lower-stem infection becomes more damaging under heat and drought.
symptoms: Premature wilting and yellowing during reproductive growth.
Fine black specks inside lower stems and roots, giving a charcoal-like appearance.
charcoal-rot.conditions: High soil temperature, drought stress, and repeated susceptible crops.
prevention: Reduce avoidable moisture stress and select adapted varieties.
Use balanced nutrition and discuss rotation options, since the pathogen has many hosts.
management: Manage irrigation carefully where available and avoid further root stress.
Confirm the disease through stem and root examination; dead tissue cannot be restored.

yellow-mosaic.name: Yellow Mosaic
yellow-mosaic.description: Mottled yellow leaves can signal a whitefly-transmitted virus.
symptoms: Irregular yellow and green mosaic patterns on leaves.
Stunting, shortened internodes, and reduced pod production.
yellow-mosaic.cause: Yellow mosaic begomoviruses transmitted by whiteflies in affected regions.
yellow-mosaic.conditions: Whitefly activity and infected nearby crops or weeds.
prevention: Use regionally resistant varieties and manage alternate hosts.
Inspect seedlings and use locally recommended vector monitoring.
management: There is no cure for an established viral infection.
Confirm the cause and focus management on limiting spread to healthy plants.

sorghum.name: Sorghum
sorghum.description: A heat-tolerant grain and fodder crop suited to many rainfed farming systems.
sorghum.alt: A family standing in a mature sorghum field

anthracnose.name: Anthracnose
anthracnose.description: Leaf and stalk lesions can reduce plant vigor and grain filling.
symptoms: Small red or purple-bordered leaf spots with pale centers.
Dark fruiting structures in lesions and possible stalk or panicle damage.
anthracnose.cause: Colletotrichum sublineola, a fungal pathogen of sorghum.
anthracnose.conditions: Warm, wet weather and infected residues favor infection.
prevention: Use resistant varieties and healthy seed.
Rotate with suitable crops and manage infected sorghum residues.
management: Scout leaves, stalks, and panicles rather than judging from leaf color alone.
Use local disease guidance to protect vulnerable growth stages.

grain-mold.name: Grain Mold
grain-mold.description: Mold on developing grain can affect quality, germination, and food safety.
symptoms: White, pink, gray, or dark growth on grain.
Discolored, shriveled grain and sometimes poor seed germination.
grain-mold.cause: A complex of fungi including Fusarium and Curvularia species.
grain-mold.conditions: Rain and humidity during flowering, grain filling, or delayed harvest.
prevention: Choose adapted, less susceptible varieties and suitable sowing dates.
Harvest at the appropriate stage and dry grain promptly.
management: Keep moldy grain separate and follow local food- and feed-safety advice.
Do not assume visibly affected grain is safe after drying or processing.

downy-mildew.name: Downy Mildew
downy-mildew.description: Systemic infection can stripe leaves and prevent normal head formation.
symptoms: Pale stripes on leaves, sometimes with downy growth beneath.
Leaves may shred; affected plants can be stunted or sterile.
downy-mildew.conditions: Humid nights and inoculum in soil or nearby infected plants.
prevention: Use resistant hybrids and reliable seed sources.
Rotate and manage volunteer plants according to local guidance.
management: Confirm the diagnosis where pale stripes first appear.
Avoid saving seed from severely affected fields and review local planting recommendations.

sunflower.name: Sunflower
sunflower.description: A sun-loving oilseed with deep roots, suited to well-drained black and loamy soils.
sunflower.alt: A field of blooming yellow sunflowers at sunset

alternaria-leaf-spot.name: Alternaria Leaf Spot
alternaria-leaf-spot.description: Dark leaf lesions can merge and reduce healthy leaf area.
symptoms: Dark brown spots, sometimes with concentric rings and yellow halos.
Lesions on stems or heads and premature leaf drying.
alternaria-leaf-spot.cause: Alternaria helianthi and related fungi affecting sunflower.
alternaria-leaf-spot.conditions: Warm weather, rain, and extended leaf wetness.
prevention: Use healthy seed, suitable rotation, and recommended spacing.
Manage infected residues and avoid unnecessary overhead wetting.
management: Inspect both lower and upper leaves as the crop develops.
Have lesions distinguished from other sunflower spots before choosing management.

downy-mildew.name: Downy Mildew
downy-mildew.description: Early infection can produce stunted plants with pale, thickened leaves.
symptoms: Pale areas along leaf veins and downy growth beneath leaves.
Stunting and small or poorly developed flower heads.
downy-mildew.conditions: Cool, wet soil around establishment and susceptible hybrids.
prevention: Choose locally resistant hybrids and certified seed.
Use well-drained fields and suitable crop rotations.
management: Check stunted plants early rather than waiting until flowering.
Consult local experts about approved seed-health measures for future crops.

rust.name: Rust
rust.description: Rust pustules reduce leaf function when the canopy becomes heavily infected.
symptoms: Small cinnamon-brown pustules on leaves, especially underneath.
Pustules can darken as plants mature; severe leaves dry early.
rust.cause: Puccinia helianthi, the sunflower rust fungus.
rust.conditions: Warm, humid weather, dew, and volunteer sunflower hosts.
prevention: Use resistant hybrids and manage volunteer sunflowers.
Maintain balanced nutrition and recommended spacing.
management: Monitor the spread of pustules through the canopy.
Use local extension thresholds before considering crop-protection products.

groundnut.name: Groundnut
groundnut.description: A warm-season crop that prefers loose soil for peg penetration and easy lifting.
groundnut.alt: Hands holding freshly harvested groundnuts with green foliage behind

tikka-leaf-spot.name: Tikka Leaf Spot
tikka-leaf-spot.description: Early and late leaf spots can cause substantial leaf loss in groundnut.
symptoms: Brown to black circular spots on leaflets, sometimes with yellow halos.
Premature shedding of leaves and reduced canopy cover.
tikka-leaf-spot.cause: Early and late leaf-spot fungi, commonly referred to as Cercospora and Phaeoisariopsis complexes.
tikka-leaf-spot.conditions: Warm, humid conditions, frequent rain, and infected groundnut residues.
prevention: Use recommended tolerant varieties and healthy seed.
Rotate with suitable non-host crops and manage residues after harvest.
management: Monitor leaves from the lower canopy upward, including during pod filling.
Use locally recommended disease thresholds and confirm whether rust is also present.

rust.name: Rust
rust.description: Orange pustules can develop alongside leaf spot and accelerate leaf drying.
symptoms: Small orange-brown pustules, mostly beneath leaflets.
Leaves become dry and brittle during severe infection.
rust.cause: Puccinia arachidis, a groundnut-specific rust fungus.
rust.conditions: Humid weather, moderate temperatures, and living infected host plants nearby.
prevention: Choose recommended resistant varieties where available.
Manage volunteer groundnut and follow locally suitable sowing dates.
management: Inspect leaf undersides and distinguish rust from ordinary leaf spots.
Ask an adviser to assess combined rust and leaf-spot pressure.

stem-rot.name: Stem Rot
stem-rot.description: A soil-borne fungus attacks stems near the soil surface and can rot pods.
symptoms: Wilting branches with white fungal growth near the stem base.
Small mustard-seed-like fungal bodies and rotting pods.
stem-rot.cause: Athelia rolfsii, commonly called Sclerotium rolfsii.
stem-rot.conditions: Warm, moist soil and infected organic debris around plant bases.
prevention: Improve drainage and use suitable rotations.
Avoid moving contaminated soil or leaving diseased residues around new plants.
management: Have affected stem bases and pods examined for confirmation.
Manage irrigation carefully and seek local integrated soil-disease recommendations.

millets.name: Millets
millets.description: A resilient rainfed cereal. This guide focuses on pearl millet in warm regions.
millets.alt: Pearl millet heads growing in a lush green field

downy-mildew.name: Downy Mildew
downy-mildew.description: The green-ear disease can transform flower parts into leafy structures.
symptoms: Yellowing or striped leaves with downy growth in humid conditions.
Leafy, malformed heads known as green ears.
downy-mildew.cause: Sclerospora graminicola, an oomycete pathogen of pearl millet.
downy-mildew.conditions: Humid weather, susceptible hybrids, and persistent field inoculum.
prevention: Use resistant hybrids and certified healthy seed.
Rotate crops and manage volunteer millet.
management: Inspect seedlings and developing heads for early symptoms.
Do not save seed from severely affected plants; ask about locally approved seed-health practices.

ergot.name: Ergot
ergot.description: Flower infection produces honeydew and hard fungal structures in place of grain.
symptoms: Sticky honeydew droplets from florets during flowering.
Dark, hard structures replacing some grains at maturity.
ergot.cause: Claviceps fusiformis, an ergot fungus affecting pearl millet.
ergot.conditions: Cool, humid weather around flowering and poorly synchronized pollination.
prevention: Use clean seed and recommended varieties and planting dates.
Prevent contaminated grain from being used as seed.
management: Keep contaminated grain separate and seek food- and feed-safety guidance.
Do not eat or feed ergot-contaminated grain to animals.

smut.name: Smut
smut.description: Infected grains become enlarged sacs containing dark spores.
symptoms: Enlarged green-to-brown sacs instead of normal kernels.
Sacs split to release dark powdery spores.
smut.cause: Moesziomyces penicillariae, the pearl millet smut fungus.
smut.conditions: Humid weather during flowering and susceptible varieties.
prevention: Use recommended resistant hybrids and healthy seed.
Avoid using grain from visibly infected heads for sowing.
management: Confirm the disease at head development.
Reduce spore spread during handling and consult local crop-sanitation guidance.

potato.name: Potato
potato.description: A cool-season crop that needs loose, fertile soil and even moisture for tuber growth.
potato.alt: Harvested potatoes moving through a sorting conveyor

late-blight.name: Late Blight
late-blight.description: A rapidly spreading leaf and tuber disease during cool, wet weather.
symptoms: Water-soaked leaf lesions that quickly turn brown or black.
White growth at lesion margins in humid weather; brown, firm tuber rot.
late-blight.cause: Phytophthora infestans, an oomycete rather than a true fungus.
late-blight.conditions: Cool, wet periods with prolonged humidity and infected seed tubers or volunteers.
prevention: Use certified healthy seed tubers and locally resistant varieties.
Remove volunteer plants and manage cull piles safely.
management: Scout frequently during local blight alerts and seek advice promptly.
Separate suspect tubers and avoid storing damaged or wet produce.

early-blight.name: Early Blight
early-blight.description: Target-like leaf lesions often develop on older or stressed foliage.
symptoms: Brown spots with concentric rings, especially on lower leaves.
Yellowing around lesions and gradual loss of foliage.
early-blight.cause: Alternaria solani and related early-blight fungi.
early-blight.conditions: Warm weather, alternating wet and dry periods, and stressed or aging plants.
prevention: Rotate crops and manage infected residues.
Maintain balanced nutrition and consistent irrigation.
management: Inspect the lesion pattern and distinguish early from late blight.
Reduce crop stress and follow locally appropriate management advice.

common-scab.name: Common Scab
common-scab.description: Corky tuber lesions reduce appearance and market quality.
symptoms: Raised, shallow, or deep-pitted corky scabs on tuber skin.
The above-ground plant may appear healthy.
common-scab.cause: Pathogenic Streptomyces bacteria living in soil.
common-scab.conditions: Dry conditions during early tuber formation and some higher-pH soils favor scab.
prevention: Use healthy seed tubers and less susceptible varieties.
Maintain appropriate moisture during tuber initiation and manage amendments using soil-test advice.
management: Do not use heavily scabbed tubers for planting.
Have scab differentiated from powdery scab and other tuber disorders.

watermelon.name: Watermelon
watermelon.description: A sun-loving summer crop suited to sandy loam with reliable, well-managed irrigation.
watermelon.alt: Ripe green watermelons lying among leaves in a farm field

fusarium-wilt.name: Fusarium Wilt
fusarium-wilt.description: A soil-borne vascular disease that can wilt vines before harvest.
symptoms: Wilting of individual runners, followed by wider vine decline.
Brown discoloration inside affected stems near the base.
fusarium-wilt.cause: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. niveum; pathogen races vary in affected regions.
fusarium-wilt.conditions: Infested soils, susceptible varieties, and root stress.
prevention: Use resistant varieties or locally recommended grafted plants.
Rotate away from watermelon and avoid moving contaminated soil.
management: Confirm the cause before treating, because drought and root damage also cause wilt.
Improve root-zone conditions and review the next crop plan with an adviser.

anthracnose.name: Anthracnose
anthracnose.description: Leaf spotting and sunken fruit lesions can reduce marketable yield.
symptoms: Dark irregular spots on leaves and elongated stem lesions.
Sunken fruit spots that may develop pinkish spore masses.
anthracnose.cause: Colletotrichum orbiculare, a cucurbit anthracnose fungus.
anthracnose.conditions: Warm, wet weather and splash dispersal from infected material.
prevention: Use healthy seed and resistant varieties where available.
Avoid working in wet crops and rotate with non-cucurbit crops.
management: Remove affected fruit from harvest lots and handle produce carefully.
Have fruit lesions diagnosed and use local integrated disease advice.

powdery-mildew.name: Powdery Mildew
powdery-mildew.description: Powdery patches can weaken leaves and expose fruit to sun damage.
symptoms: White powdery patches on leaves and petioles.
Yellowing, drying leaves, and reduced canopy protection.
powdery-mildew.cause: Powdery-mildew fungi such as Podosphaera xanthii.
powdery-mildew.conditions: Warm conditions, humid nights, and dense leaf canopies.
prevention: Use suitable spacing and recommended tolerant varieties.
Avoid excessive nitrogen and maintain healthy growth.
management: Inspect older leaves regularly.
Reduce avoidable crop stress and seek local guidance before applying protection products.

coconut.name: Coconut
coconut.description: A tropical palm for warm, frost-free areas with good drainage and adequate moisture.
coconut.alt: Clusters of green coconuts growing on a palm tree

bud-rot.name: Bud Rot
bud-rot.description: Infection of the growing point can threaten survival of a palm.
symptoms: Yellowing or wilting of the young central spear leaf.
Soft, foul-smelling tissue in the crown; the spear may pull out easily.
bud-rot.cause: Frequently Phytophthora palmivora, an oomycete, though crown rots require diagnosis.
bud-rot.conditions: Prolonged wet weather and moisture accumulation in the crown.
prevention: Improve drainage and avoid crown injuries.
Inspect young palms and palms in affected areas during rainy periods.
management: Get expert help promptly because the growing point is vital.
Do not attempt unsafe climbing or invasive crown treatment without trained assistance.

stem-bleeding.name: Stem Bleeding
stem-bleeding.description: Dark exudation from trunk lesions can accompany internal decay.
symptoms: Reddish-brown liquid oozing from cracks or patches on the trunk.
Darkened underlying tissue and reduced vigor in severe cases.
stem-bleeding.cause: Often Thielaviopsis-associated fungal infection, commonly linked with trunk injury.
stem-bleeding.conditions: Injuries, moisture imbalance, and weak or stressed palms.
prevention: Avoid trunk wounds and maintain balanced nutrition.
Use consistent moisture management and good basin drainage.
management: Ask a trained agricultural professional to assess lesion depth.
Do not cut or scrape the trunk indiscriminately; intervention depends on confirmed severity.

root-wilt-disease.name: Root Wilt Disease
root-wilt-disease.description: A chronic palm decline that requires long-term integrated management.
symptoms: Flaccid or ribbed leaflets and yellowing of older leaves.
Reduced nut production and shedding of immature nuts.
root-wilt-disease.cause: A phytoplasma-associated disease occurring in affected coconut-growing regions.
root-wilt-disease.conditions: Local vector transmission and plant stress can influence severity.
prevention: Source healthy seedlings and follow regional planting guidance.
Maintain drainage, nutrition, and recommended intercrop practices.
management: There is no simple spray cure for an infected palm.
Use locally recommended integrated management and seek diagnosis before deciding to remove a palm.

cashew.name: Cashew
cashew.description: A hardy tropical tree grown on well-drained uplands, including improved lateritic soils.
cashew.alt: A ripe red cashew apple and attached nut growing on a tree

anthracnose.name: Anthracnose
anthracnose.description: A wet-weather disease affecting shoots, flowers, and developing fruit.
symptoms: Dark sunken spots on young leaves, shoots, and fruit.
Blighted flowers and dieback of tender shoots.
anthracnose.cause: Colletotrichum species associated with cashew anthracnose.
anthracnose.conditions: Warm, wet weather, dense crowns, and infected plant debris.
prevention: Maintain appropriate spacing and prune for air circulation.
Use healthy nursery plants and remove infected material as locally advised.
management: Monitor flowering and new growth during rainy spells.
Confirm the cause of flower loss before choosing management.

powdery-mildew.name: Powdery Mildew
powdery-mildew.description: Powdery colonies on tender growth can affect flowering and fruit set.
symptoms: White or gray powder on young leaves and flower panicles.
Distorted young growth and poor fruit set.
powdery-mildew.cause: Powdery-mildew fungi affecting cashew, varying by growing region.
powdery-mildew.conditions: Humid nights, suitable mild temperatures, and tender new growth.
prevention: Maintain an open, healthy canopy.
Avoid excessive nitrogen and follow regionally recommended orchard practices.
management: Inspect tender growth and flower panicles regularly.
Seek local advice on protecting flowering rather than assuming all flower drop is disease.

dieback.name: Dieback
dieback.description: Progressive death of twigs can reduce healthy flowering wood.
symptoms: Shoots dry from the tip backward.
Darkened twigs, bark lesions, or sparse new growth.
dieback.cause: Several fungi, including Lasiodiplodia species, can be involved; stress and wounds contribute.
dieback.conditions: Plant stress, poor nutrition, and infection through injured tissues.
prevention: Use clean pruning tools and avoid unnecessary wounds.
Maintain balanced nutrition and appropriate moisture.
management: Ask an adviser to distinguish fungal dieback from pest damage or drought.
Prune affected wood only with appropriate sanitation and local guidance.

tea.name: Tea
tea.description: A perennial crop for humid regions with acidic, well-drained soil and suitable temperatures.
tea.alt: Rolling green tea plantations seen from above

blister-blight.name: Blister Blight
blister-blight.description: Young leaves develop blisters that reduce the quality of harvestable shoots.
symptoms: Pale translucent spots on tender leaves.
Raised blisters, often with white growth beneath, and distorted young leaves.
blister-blight.cause: Exobasidium vexans, the tea blister-blight fungus.
blister-blight.conditions: Cool, misty conditions and prolonged wetness on young shoots.
prevention: Regulate shade and maintain airflow in tea bushes.
Use locally recommended plucking and canopy-management practices.
management: Monitor new flush during humid periods.
Follow guidance from local tea research or extension services, including harvest-safety requirements.

grey-blight.name: Grey Blight
grey-blight.description: Blighted leaf tissue can develop after injury or stress.
symptoms: Brown spots enlarging into gray-centered areas.
Small dark fungal structures in dead tissue and leaf drying.
grey-blight.cause: Pestalotiopsis and related fungi associated with tea gray blight.
grey-blight.conditions: Warm, wet conditions, damaged foliage, and stressed bushes.
prevention: Minimize leaf injury and keep pruning and harvesting tools clean.
Maintain balanced nutrition and suitable shade.
management: Confirm the cause of leaf damage and address stress factors.
Follow tea-specific advice before using any crop-protection product on harvestable shoots.

red-rust.name: Red Rust
red-rust.description: Orange-red growth on stems or leaves can indicate an algal infection.
symptoms: Rust-colored, velvety patches on leaves or young stems.
Reduced shoot vigor where infection is severe.
red-rust.cause: Cephaleuros species, parasitic algae; this is not the same as cereal rust.
red-rust.conditions: Persistent humidity, weak bushes, and excessive shade.
prevention: Improve plant vigor with balanced nutrition.
Regulate shade and maintain airflow.
management: Have the algal cause confirmed before choosing a control approach.
Use local tea-extension guidance and correct the conditions stressing the bushes.

tomato.name: Tomato
tomato.description: A rewarding fruiting vegetable that prefers fertile loam and steady, even moisture.
tomato.alt: Ripe red tomatoes hanging on a vine

early-blight.name: Early Blight
early-blight.description: Target-like leaf spots often begin on older tomato leaves.
symptoms: Brown lesions with concentric rings on lower leaves.
Yellowing around spots and gradual leaf loss.
early-blight.cause: Alternaria solani and related Alternaria species.
early-blight.conditions: Warm temperatures, leaf wetness, and nutrient or moisture stress.
prevention: Use healthy transplants, suitable rotations, and clean supports.
Keep leaves dry where possible and maintain balanced nutrition.
management: Remove severely affected leaves when practical without over-defoliating the plant.
Distinguish early blight from late blight and other spots before intervention.

late-blight.name: Late Blight
late-blight.description: Fast-spreading lesions can damage leaves, stems, and fruit in wet weather.
symptoms: Irregular water-soaked lesions that rapidly turn brown-black.
White growth along lesion edges in humid weather; firm brown fruit lesions.
late-blight.cause: Phytophthora infestans, an oomycete pathogen shared with potato.
late-blight.conditions: Cool, wet spells, prolonged humidity, and infected neighboring crops.
prevention: Use healthy seedlings and locally suitable resistant varieties.
Improve airflow and manage volunteer tomato and potato plants.
management: Seek a diagnosis quickly during local blight alerts.
Avoid handling wet infected plants and keep affected fruit out of storage lots.

bacterial-wilt.name: Bacterial Wilt
bacterial-wilt.description: A soil-borne vascular infection can cause sudden, permanent wilting.
symptoms: Wilting while leaves may remain green at first.
Brown internal stem tissue; bacterial ooze may be present in cut stems.
bacterial-wilt.conditions: Warm, moist soil, root injury, contaminated water, and susceptible plants.
prevention: Use clean seedlings and locally recommended resistant rootstocks where available.
Improve drainage and avoid moving contaminated soil or water.
management: Confirm the cause, since fungal wilt and water stress can look similar.
There is no reliable field cure for an established infection; prevent spread and plan suitable rotation.

powdery-mildew.name: Powdery Mildew
powdery-mildew.description: Powdery growth or yellow patches can reduce the healthy tomato canopy.
symptoms: White powdery patches or yellow areas on leaves, depending on the pathogen.
Progressive leaf drying and reduced canopy cover.
powdery-mildew.cause: Powdery-mildew fungi including Leveillula and Oidium-related species.
powdery-mildew.conditions: Warm to mild conditions, humid periods, and dense foliage.
prevention: Provide suitable spacing and manage canopy density.
Avoid excess nitrogen and choose adapted varieties.
management: Inspect leaf undersides as well as upper surfaces.
Get local advice on the specific mildew type before choosing management.

leaf-curl.name: Leaf Curl
leaf-curl.description: A viral disease that can curl and yellow young leaves and reduce fruit set.
symptoms: Upward curling, yellow margins, and thickened or small young leaves.
Stunting and poor flower or fruit development.
leaf-curl.cause: Tomato leaf-curl begomoviruses, commonly transmitted by whiteflies.
leaf-curl.conditions: High whitefly populations, infected weed hosts, and susceptible transplants.
prevention: Use healthy seedlings and locally resistant varieties.
Protect nurseries and manage whiteflies using integrated local recommendations.
management: There is no spray that cures a plant of an established leaf-curl virus.
Have viral leaf curl distinguished from heat or water-stress curling; focus on protecting healthy plants.

chickpea.name: Chickpea
chickpea.description: A cool-season legume often grown on stored soil moisture with good drainage.
chickpea.alt: A close view of harvested chickpeas

fusarium-wilt.name: Fusarium Wilt
fusarium-wilt.description: A soil-borne vascular disease causing wilt in seedlings or mature plants.
symptoms: Drooping leaves and plant collapse in patches.
Brown discoloration inside roots and lower stems.
fusarium-wilt.cause: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. ciceris, with different races present across regions.
fusarium-wilt.conditions: Infested soil, susceptible varieties, and warm soil conditions.
prevention: Use locally resistant varieties and healthy seed.
Rotate as recommended and avoid transferring soil from affected fields.
management: Confirm wilt through root and stem examination.
Improve crop stress management and seek advice for reducing risk in the next crop.

ascochyta-blight.name: Ascochyta Blight
ascochyta-blight.description: A wet-weather blight affecting leaves, stems, and pods.
symptoms: Brown lesions with tiny dark dots arranged in rings.
Stem breakage at lesions and spotting on pods or seed.
ascochyta-blight.cause: Ascochyta rabiei, a seed- and residue-borne fungus.
ascochyta-blight.conditions: Cool, wet weather, rain splash, and infected seed or residues.
prevention: Use healthy seed and resistant varieties where available.
Rotate crops and avoid planting next to infected chickpea residues.
management: Scout after rainy periods and avoid moving through wet crops.
Have symptoms confirmed promptly when stem lesions appear.

dry-root-rot.name: Dry Root Rot
dry-root-rot.description: Root decay becomes particularly damaging during hot, dry conditions.
symptoms: Rapid drying of plants around flowering or pod filling.
Brittle dark roots with fine black fungal structures and few side roots.
dry-root-rot.cause: Macrophomina phaseolina, also known by its older name Rhizoctonia bataticola.
dry-root-rot.conditions: High temperatures and moisture stress, especially later in the crop.
prevention: Use adapted varieties and suitable sowing dates.
Reduce avoidable moisture stress and maintain balanced soil nutrition.
management: Examine roots to distinguish this disease from other wilts.
Discuss moisture and rotation management with a local adviser; dead root tissue cannot recover.

mustard.name: Mustard
mustard.description: A cool-season oilseed suited to well-drained loam and carefully managed clay loam.
mustard.alt: A field of yellow-flowering brassica plants

white-rust.name: White Rust
white-rust.description: White pustules and distorted flower heads can reduce seed production.
symptoms: Raised white pustules on lower leaf surfaces.
Swollen, twisted flower stalks sometimes called stagheads.
white-rust.cause: Albugo candida, an oomycete; it is distinct from true fungal rusts.
white-rust.conditions: Cool, humid weather and infected brassica crops or weeds nearby.
prevention: Use resistant varieties and suitable crop rotation.
Manage brassica weed hosts and plant healthy seed.
management: Inspect the undersides of leaves and developing flower heads.
Confirm white rust and any accompanying downy mildew with a local adviser.

alternaria-blight.name: Alternaria Blight
alternaria-blight.description: Dark spots on leaves and pods may affect seed quality and yield.
symptoms: Brown-black circular spots with concentric rings on leaves.
Dark pod lesions and premature pod drying or seed damage.
alternaria-blight.conditions: Humid weather, dew, and infected seed or residues.
prevention: Use healthy seed and rotate away from susceptible brassicas.
Follow recommended sowing dates and manage crop residues.
management: Monitor both foliage and pods as the crop matures.
Seek local advice on severity and harvest timing rather than relying only on leaf symptoms.

downy-mildew.name: Downy Mildew
downy-mildew.description: Leaf infection can weaken seedlings and affect older foliage in cool weather.
symptoms: Pale or yellow patches on upper leaf surfaces.
White-gray downy growth beneath affected areas.
downy-mildew.conditions: Cool, moist weather and extended humidity around leaves.
prevention: Use clean planting material and avoid overly dense stands.
Manage infected brassica residues and weed hosts.
management: Inspect young plants early and confirm the cause of yellowing.
Improve airflow and follow local integrated management guidance.
